title: AI adoption happens at separate firm, business-function, and worker-task layers
source_unit: Census CES Working Paper 26-25 using the 2026 AI supplement to the Business Trends and Outlook Survey
geography: United States; firms, business functions, employment-weighted firms, and worker tasks

observations.period: BTOS AI supplement reference period November 2025-January 2026; paper published April 2026

denominator.unit: nationally representative firm survey with employment-weighted comparisons

firm_function_use.value: 18% of firms used AI in a business function; 32% employment-weighted

expected_adoption.value: adoption was expected to reach 22% within six months

worker_task_use.value: 23% of firms reported workers using AI in work-related tasks; 41% employment-weighted

limited_scope.value: 57% of adopting firms used AI in three or fewer business functions and 65% used it in three or fewer tasks

augmentation.value: 66% of users relied on AI solely to augment tasks; AI-related employment decreases occurred in 2% of firms

layer_divergence.value: worker task use sometimes occurred without formal firm adoption, and firm adoption sometimes occurred without worker task use

performance.value: broader AI integration was positively correlated with commercial performance; functional breadth and operational investment were associated with employment decreases, while worker-task integration was not significantly linked to headcount reduction after controls

observations.method: The authors use nationally representative BTOS AI-supplement data to measure firm use, business-function deployment, and worker-task use, then estimate correlations with commercial performance and employment outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census CES working paper and not a Census Bureau endorsement. The survey is mainly a firm-level cross-section for the stated reference period; the correlations do not establish that AI caused performance or employment changes, and employment-weighted and firm-weighted rates answer different questions.
observations.subgroup: Firms by size and sector, especially Information, Professional Services, and Finance; functional and task differences are reported, but worker-level exposure, wages, schedules, job quality, and unequal effects by race, gender, age, or occupation are not fully identified in the abstract.
observations.counterinterpretation: Larger firms may both adopt AI and have greater resources, performance, or reporting capacity. AI use can augment, reorganize, or replace work; low observed employment decreases may reflect timing, measurement, internal reassignment, or later effects. Commercial performance is not worker wellbeing or consumer benefit.

related_sources.claim: The official paper provides the BTOS design, layer definitions, adoption rates, and firm-performance and employment associations.

boundary: This record adds a three-layer AI diffusion map from firms to functions to tasks. It does not establish causality, worker-level wellbeing, job displacement, productivity sharing, consumer outcomes, or durable control over AI systems.
